newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung assures on freedom, sees closer China links.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung assures on freedom, sees closer China links.

text.p: Freedom and prosperity will continue in Hong Kong after China takes over on July 1, but the territory's links to the communist-ruled mainland will continue to grow closer, Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa said on Thursday.

"The long-term interests of Hong Kong and China are the same," Tung said in a live broadcast on Cable News Network (CNN). "What is good for Hong Kong is good for China and what is good for China is very good for Hong Kong."

Repeating assurances made during his leadership campaign last year, Tung stressed Hong Kong's economic might and the confidence of its 6.4 million people in a smooth transition to Chinese sovereignty after 156 years of British colonial rule.

"We as Chinese people see the handover as a coming together, a natural reconciliation ending a long period of separation," said Tung, who was picked to lead post-handover Hong Kong by a 400-member, Beijing-backed committee.
It was the second time this week that Tung had appeared on a U.S. news programme to talk about the future of the bustling, capitalist territory.

On Tuesday, Tung vowed on ABC News's "Nightline" to protect the right to protest and declared he would "not allow" suppression of dissent like the violent crushing of 1989's student-led protests centred on Beijing's Tiananmen Square.

Debate on the future of political freedoms and civil rights heated up over the past few weeks during public consultations on Tung's plan to tighten laws covering the right to protest and funding for political groups.
Tung proposed the curbs after China's parliament declared parts of the two Public Order and Societies laws incompatible with the Basic Law, Beijing's mini-constitution for Hong Kong.

"Debate over these proposals is appropriate. Exaggeration of their impact on civil liberties is not," Tung told CNN, adding that individual rights must be balanced against social order and the greater good of the community.

Tung's appearance on CNN came a day after the deadline for comments on his plan to amend civil liberties laws. More than 4,000 submissions had been received by Wednesday evening, a spokesman for Tung said.
Pro-democracy parties, lawyers, human rights groups, unions and churches objected to Tung's plan in written submissions.
Groups representing industry, commerce, pro-China parties and pro-Beijing trade unions have declared support.
Tung's future Justice Secretary Elsie Leung said she expected the amendments to be drafted into a proposed law by the middle of next month, Radio Hong Kong reported.
The concerns raised by the international community about civil liberties in Hong Kong after the handover were those of the territory's people, Tung told CNN.
"We want our freedom preserved, we want democracy to move ahead, we want our economic vitality," he said.
Beijing has promised Hong Kong a large degree of autonomy after the handover, allowing it to retain its capitalist system for 50 years.
